articles.full_text:
As global temperatures climb, scientists are increasingly warning that the health consequences of a warming planet extend far beyond heatstroke and dehydration. Now, a sweeping new analysis suggests that one of the most intimate casualties of extreme heat may be human fertility itself. In a study published in Frontiers in Public Health, researchers report that countries exposed to more days of very strong and extreme heat stress show significantly higher prevalence of infertility, with the association appearing strongest for women and for populations living in the world’s most vulnerable regions.
The investigation, led by Dian Wang of the First Affiliated Hospital of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University and colleagues, is what epidemiologists call an ecological study: rather than tracking individuals, it examines population-level patterns across entire countries. The team analyzed data from 174 countries and regions over a 31-year period, from 1990 to 2021, making it one of the largest attempts to date to characterize the relationship between heat exposure and infertility at a global scale. Infertility already affects an estimated 10 to 15 percent of couples of reproductive age worldwide, and fertility rates in many countries have fallen below replacement levels, raising concerns about demographic and socioeconomic consequences.
What sets this study apart technically is its choice of exposure metric. Most previous research on temperature and reproduction has relied on ambient air temperature or simplified thermal indices as proxies for what the human body actually experiences. The researchers instead used the Universal Thermal Climate Index, or UTCI, a physiologically grounded measure developed in biometeorology that integrates air temperature, humidity, wind, and radiation into a single equivalent temperature under standardized reference conditions. In other words, UTCI estimates the air temperature at which a person would experience the same physiological strain as under the actual, combined meteorological conditions. The index is considered robust across different climates, seasons, and spatial scales, from microenvironments to global assessments, and is already used in public meteorological services and health warning systems.
To quantify exposure, the team drew on ERA5-HEAT, the first global historical gridded dataset built on a human biometeorological index, produced by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts and available through the Copernicus Climate Data Store. The dataset provides hourly UTCI estimates at a resolution of 0.25 by 0.25 degrees of latitude and longitude. For each grid cell and each year, the researchers counted the number of days on which the daily maximum UTCI fell into four established heat stress categories: moderate, corresponding to UTCI values of 26 to 32 degrees Celsius; strong, from 32 to 38 degrees; very strong, from 38 to 46 degrees; and extreme, above 46 degrees. These counts were then averaged within national boundaries to produce country-level annual exposure estimates.
Infertility prevalence data came from the Global Burden of Disease study, which models age-standardized prevalence rates, or ASPRs, for male and female infertility as separate outcomes using a Bayesian meta-regression framework that integrates population-based reproductive surveys, mainly among married or cohabiting women. Because such surveys cannot directly identify the responsible partner, the GBD framework generates sex-specific estimates informed by epidemiological evidence and prior attribution patterns. The researchers also adjusted their statistical models for the Socio-demographic Index, a composite measure of income, education, and fertility, as well as for ambient air pollution exposures including particulate matter, nitrogen dioxide, and ozone.
The statistical machinery was correspondingly elaborate. The team applied Geodetector, a spatial analysis method, to test whether the number of heat-stress days explained geographic variation in infertility prevalence, finding modest but statistically significant spatial associations for both sexes. They then trained an XGBoost machine-learning model on 5,568 country-year observations and interpreted it using SHapley Additive exPlanations, or SHAP, which assigns each predictor an additive contribution to the model’s output. Heat-stress days ranked among the relatively more important variables explaining variation in infertility prevalence for both men and women. The core analysis used linear mixed-effects models with country as a random intercept, adjusted for the Socio-demographic Index, the three air pollutants, and calendar year, with variance inflation factors ranging from 1.56 to 2.91, indicating that multicollinearity was not a major concern.
The headline results are striking. Each additional day of very strong heat stress was associated with an increase in male infertility ASPR of 1.292 per 100,000 population, and each additional day of extreme heat stress with an increase of 1.654 per 100,000. For women, the corresponding figures were 2.126 and 7.133 per 100,000, meaning that a single extra day of extreme heat stress per year was associated with a female infertility burden more than four times larger than for men. Moderate heat stress was positively associated with female infertility but not significantly with male infertility, while strong heat stress showed no significant association with either sex. The researchers also constructed a weighted heat-stress score combining very strong and extreme heat stress days, using a cross-fitting strategy in which countries were randomly partitioned into ten subsets to avoid overfitting. Each one-unit increase in this score was associated with increases of 0.337 and 0.909 per 100,000 in male and female infertility prevalence, respectively.
The geographic pattern of the findings adds a troubling dimension of inequity. Globally, the average annual number of days with UTCI at or above 26 degrees was 239.84, but exposure varied enormously: countries in the low Socio-demographic Index group averaged 326.99 heat-stress days per year, compared with just 64.80 days in the high-SDI group. Heat-stress days were most frequent in tropical and subtropical regions, with Africa averaging 323.69 days and low-latitude countries 327.85 days, while Europe averaged only 64.09 days. Subgroup analyses showed that the associations between the heat-stress score and infertility were significant in low and low-middle SDI regions, in Africa, North America, and South America, and at low and middle latitudes. The authors suggest that higher-SDI regions generally have better access to cooling infrastructure, healthcare, and protective resources, while populations in lower-SDI areas may face greater challenges in accessing such measures. Interestingly, the strongest association appeared in low-middle rather than low SDI regions, possibly because infections account for a larger share of the infertility burden in the lowest-SDI settings, diluting the relative contribution of heat.
The results align with a growing body of biological and epidemiological evidence. Studies have reported that exposure to high ambient temperatures and heatwaves is associated with poorer sperm quality, including lower sperm counts, reduced motility, and higher prevalence of abnormal morphology, likely reflecting disruption of spermatogenesis, a process known to be highly temperature-sensitive. For women, higher ambient temperatures have been linked to reduced antral follicle counts and diminished ovarian reserve, potentially affecting follicular development and ovarian function. Heat stress has also been associated with abnormalities in thyroid-stimulating hormone levels in women, suggesting endocrine pathways may contribute to the reproductive effects of heat. A nationwide pre-conception cohort study involving over 14 million Chinese couples planning a pregnancy found that heat stress exposure was associated with a longer time to pregnancy, providing individual-level support for the population patterns observed here. The authors also note that women in certain contexts may face greater heat and dehydration burdens due to gender-specific patterns of daily activity, such as unpaid household labor and water-fetching responsibilities, which may help explain the stronger associations observed among women.
The authors are careful to emphasize the limitations inherent in their design. As an ecological study, the findings describe associations at the population level and cannot establish causation for any individual. Residual confounding cannot be fully excluded, and factors such as access to assisted reproductive technology and occupational heat exposure were not available for adjustment. Infertility estimates derive from modeled epidemiological evidence rather than individual clinical assessments, and national-level averaging of heat exposure may not capture spatial variation within countries. Nevertheless, the associations remained directionally stable across a battery of sensitivity analyses, including two-way fixed-effects models with Driscoll-Kraay standard errors, log-transformed outcomes, additional adjustment for population density, life expectancy, urbanization, and smoking prevalence, and lag analyses testing delayed effects. With the frequency and intensity of very strong and extreme heat stress projected to increase under ongoing climate change, the authors argue that reproductive health deserves a place in climate adaptation strategies and heat-protection planning, particularly in the low-income, low-latitude regions where the burden appears greatest.

articles.full_text:
The IMC raised concerns about the impact of expected El Niño conditions, which could bring above-normal temperatures
The government has warned that millions of South Africans could face extremely high temperatures and prolonged queues when they head to voting stations for the 4 November local government elections.
The warning came after the Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) on Local Government Elections met on Friday to assess preparations for the elections and the country’s expected summer weather conditions.
Cooperative Governance and Traditional Affairs (Cogta) Minister Velenkosini Hlabisa convened the fortnightly meeting on 16 October, with the committee saying preparations for the elections remained on track.
However, the IMC raised concerns about the impact of expected El Niño conditions, which could bring above-normal temperatures and below-normal rainfall across large parts of the country.
Millions could stand in queues
The committee said the combination of extreme heat and long queues could pose a serious risk to voters and election officials on polling day.
“On the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events, coupled with the anticipated El Niño conditions, the IMC highlighted the urgent need to plan adequately ahead of the local government elections as millions of voters will be standing on long lines for the whole day under extremely high temperatures,” the ministry said.
The government urged communities and authorities to prepare for the conditions rather than wait for emergencies to develop.
“With these El Niño conditions already with us, we need to shift from reactive disaster response towards proactive disaster risk reduction (DRR), prevention, mitigation and preparedness,” the IMC said.
The committee warned that the expected weather would not be uniform across the country.
A strong El Niño is expected to dominate the summer season, with the main concerns being below-normal rainfall and above-normal temperatures in most parts of South Africa.
The conditions could increase the risk of drought, water shortages, agricultural losses and heat-related health impacts, while putting additional pressure on essential services.
Floods and thunderstorms still possible
Despite the broader dry and hot outlook, the government cautioned that parts of the country could still experience intense rainfall, flash floods and severe thunderstorms.
“The rainfall outlook for 26 October to 2 November 2026 indicates that spring rainfall may persist over the eastern half of the country, including the eastern Free State, Eastern Cape, North West, western Limpopo, the Mpumalanga Highveld, Gauteng and the coastal areas of the Western Cape,” it noted.
The South African Weather Service, working with the National Disaster Management Centre and others, will continue monitoring conditions and issuing updated forecasts and advisories.
The IMC urged municipalities and disaster management structures to ensure communities receive timely and localised weather warnings.
Election preparations continue
The weather warning comes as the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC) races towards Election Day, 4 November 2026, with more than 2.6 million special vote applications approved.
The IEC received a record 2 655 067 special vote applications before applications closed on 12 October, a 131% increase from 2021.
The commission has also recruited 188 500 electoral staff, while 23 696 voting stations have been secured nationwide.
The IMC said it remained confident in the IEC’s ability to manage the election independently and oversee a credible electoral process.
The committee also noted that security preparations are underway through the National Joint Operational and Intelligence Structure (NatJoints), with plans covering the pre-election, election-day and post-election phases.
“Protecting lives, livelihoods, critical infrastructure and essential services must remain a strategic priority across all spheres of government,” the IMC said.

articles.full_text:
Sabti, October 17, 2026 (HOL) – Xubnaha cusub ee Baarlamaanka Dowlad-goboleedka Galmudug ayaa la dhaariyey, iyadoo Maxamed Sheekh Axmed uu si ku-meel-gaar ah ula wareegay hoggaaminta baarlamaanka, kaddib markii uu noqday xubinta ugu da’da weyn golaha oo ka kooban 89 mudane.
Maxamed Sheekh Axmed ayaa xilkan si ku-meel-gaar ah u qabanaya ilaa laga soo dooranayo guddoonka rasmiga ah ee baarlamaanka. Sida ku cad jadwalka doorashada, doorashada guddoomiyaha iyo ku-xigeennadiisa ayaa la filayaa inay dhacdo 18-ka Oktoobar, halka doorashada madaxweynaha iyo madaxweyne ku-xigeenka Galmudug loo asteeyey 22-ka Oktoobar 2026.
Baarlamaanka cusub ayaa lagu soo doortay doorasho dhacday 30-kii Sebtembar 2026, kaddib markii Maxkamadda Sare ay burisay doorashadii hore ee 30-kii Luulyo, iyadoo sabab uga dhigtay in aan loo marin habraacyadii dastuuriga ahaa iyo shuruudihii looga baahnaa doorasho xor iyo xalaal ah.
Hase yeeshee, doorashadii ku celiska ahayd ayaa iyaduna dhalisay muran siyaasadeed, kaddib markii Guddiga Madaxa-bannaan ee Doorashooyinka Qaranka iyo Soohdimaha uu ka reebay xisbiga Towfiiq, kaas oo markii hore maxkamadda u gudbiyey dacwaddii sababtay in doorashadii hore la buriyo.
Natiijada doorashada ayaa guul weyn u horseedday Xisbiga Caddaaladda iyo Midnimada (JSP), kaas oo helay 67 kursi oo ka mid ah 89-ka kursi ee baarlamaanka, taas oo sii xoojisay awoodda siyaasadeed ee xisbiga talada haya.
Marka la doorto guddoonka rasmiga ah ee baarlamaanka, waxaa xigi doona doorashada hoggaanka sare ee Galmudug. Xisbiga JSP ayaa musharrax keliya u magacaabay xilka madaxweynaha, kaas oo ah Libaan Axmed Xasan, waxaana la filayaa inuu helo taageerada aqlabiyadda baarlamaanka.
Si kastaba ha ahaatee, hannaanka doorashada cusub ayaa weli wajahaya su'aalo la xiriira hufnaanta, ka-qaybgalka siyaasadeed iyo tartanka xisbiyada, gaar ahaan muranka ka dhashay ka-reebidda xisbiga Towfiiq.

Parts of South Africa are preparing for extremely hot weather this weekend, with temperatures expected to exceed 30°C in several provinces, according to the South African Weather Service (SAWS).
The forecast warns of high temperatures across KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga, the Free State, Eastern Cape and Northern Cape, raising concerns about heat-related illnesses and increased fire danger.
In North West province, conditions are expected to remain generally fine and hot, although isolated afternoon showers and thundershowers may develop in the extreme eastern areas.
Authorities are urging residents to take precautions, including staying hydrated, avoiding prolonged exposure to direct sunlight and limiting strenuous outdoor activities during the hottest parts of the day.
Farmers have also been advised to conserve water and ensure livestock have sufficient shade and drinking water as hot conditions put additional pressure on agricultural resources.
The warning highlights broader concerns about extreme heat and climate-related risks, which have affected communities in many parts of the world in recent years.
Weather officials urge public vigilance
Residents are encouraged to monitor official weather updates and follow safety guidance, particularly in areas where elevated temperatures could increase the risk of veld fires.

Thiruvananthapuram, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad and Kannur districts are under the orange alert, while a yellow alert has been sounded for the remaining nine districts
Thiruvananthapuram: The IMD issued an orange alert in five districts of Keralam on Saturday, warning of isolated very heavy rainfall accompanied by thunderstorms.
Thiruvananthapuram, Malappuram, Kozhikode, Wayanad and Kannur districts are under the orange alert, while a yellow alert has been sounded for the remaining nine districts, according to the latest update of the India Meteorological Department (IMD).
The yellow alert covers Kollam, Pathanamthitta, Alappuzha, Kottayam, Idukki, Ernakulam, Thrissur, Palakkad and Kasaragod districts, where isolated heavy rainfall is likely.
The IMD defines very heavy rainfall as precipitation between 115.6 mm and 204.4 mm in 24 hours, while heavy rainfall refers to 64.5 mm to 115.5 mm during the same period.
In the wake of heavy rains alert, the Kerala State Disaster Management Authority (KSDMA) has urged people living in landslide-prone areas and locations vulnerable to flash floods to move to safer places in accordance with the instructions of authorities.
Residents living along riverbanks and in areas downstream of dams have also been advised to take precautionary measures and relocate if directed by officials.
The authority asked people in vulnerable areas to identify relief camps and move to them during daylight, in coordination with local self-government and revenue officials.
It also cautioned people against crossing rivers, entering water bodies for bathing or fishing, and undertaking non-essential travel during heavy rainfall.
Tourist trips to waterfalls, water bodies and hilly areas should be avoided until the rain alerts are withdrawn, it said, adding that people should exercise caution while travelling along roads near water bodies and avoid driving through flooded stretches.
The KSDMA also warned of possible accidents due to trees, electric poles, signboards and walls collapsing amid strong winds.
District and taluk-level control rooms are operational round the clock. People can contact the toll-free numbers 1077 and 1070 for assistance, the authority said.
The alerts may be revised depending on changes in the IMD forecast, it added.

articles.full_text:
The India Meteorological Department has issued a yellow alert for Sindhudurg, Satara, Sangli, Kolhapur, Solapur and Dharashiv, forecasting rain accompanied by thunderstorms and strong winds in parts of Maharashtra on October 17. The warning comes as the state continues to experience sharp fluctuations in maximum temperatures, with several locations recording readings above 35 degrees Celsius.
The forecast covers western Maharashtra, south Konkan and parts of south Marathwada. The weather department has also warned of hot and humid conditions in Konkan, while Thane, Mumbai and Raigad are expected to experience a rise in heat and humidity. Isolated thunderstorms and rain are possible in Ratnagiri, Pune, Latur and Nanded districts.
The alert is significant for cities and towns where sudden thunderstorms can affect road travel, outdoor work, power infrastructure and local drainage systems. The forecast indicates that hot conditions and storm activity may occur within the same weather system, creating rapidly changing conditions during the day.
The weather department has linked the developing conditions to several atmospheric systems over peninsular India. A cyclonic circulation is present along the Tamil Nadu coast between 3.1 and 4.5 kilometres above the surface, while another circulation is located along the Andhra Pradesh coast at an altitude of about 1.5 kilometres. A low-pressure trough extends from this system towards south Tamil Nadu.
A separate cyclonic circulation has also been observed over the southeast Arabian Sea near the Lakshadweep Islands at about 5.8 kilometres above sea level. These systems are contributing to conditions favourable for rain and thunderstorms over parts of Maharashtra, according to the report published by Sakal.
The state’s recent temperature readings show the contrast between the heat and the expected storm activity. In the 24 hours up to Friday morning, Yavatmal recorded the highest maximum temperature in the state at 38.6 degrees Celsius. Ratnagiri recorded more than 38 degrees, while Santacruz recorded above 37 degrees. Solapur, Dhule, Jalgaon, Amravati and Chandrapur also recorded temperatures above 36 degrees.
The lowest minimum temperature in the state was 16 degrees Celsius at the Wheat Research Centre in Niphad. The wide variation between the highest and lowest readings reflects the different weather conditions developing across Maharashtra’s coastal, western and inland regions.
The yellow alert indicates that residents and local authorities in the affected districts should remain watchful as the forecast period progresses. The weather department’s next updates will determine whether the warning is extended, revised or intensified for any district.

During a review meeting at the District Collector's Office, Sunetra Pawar, who is also Beed district guardian minister, asked officials to speed up crop damage assessments, ensure transparency in crop insurance claims and prioritise drinking water supplies
Sunetra Pawar directed officials to complete crop damage assessments promptly and accelerate further action once the reports are received. Pic/Special Arrangement
Maharashtra Deputy Chief Minister Sunetra Ajit Pawar reviewed the severe drought situation in Beed district on Saturday and directed officials to take urgent steps to provide relief to farmers and residents facing crop losses, drinking water shortages and a lack of fodder for livestock, an official statement said.
During a review meeting at the District Collector's Office, Sunetra Pawar, who is also Beed district guardian minister, asked officials to speed up crop damage assessments, ensure transparency in crop insurance claims and prioritise drinking water supplies. The district is currently receiving water through 225 tankers, according to information shared at the meeting.
